extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in philosophy of science, physics, and scientific methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging scientific conceptions (e.g., geometry, atom, ether, space, time): when to postulate them, how to treat their reality-status, and the limits of their applicability for classifying and predicting sense-impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of scientific conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Their validity lies in the power they give us of codifying past and predicting future experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometrical definitions and physical conceptions (atom, ether, etc.) are 'pure conceptions' or 'ideal symbols' that enable approximate analysis of sense-impressions. They do not correspond with absolute reality but are judged by their descriptive and predictive utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific conceptions as useful ideals (do not assert perceptual reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical surface, atom, ether, exist only in the human mind, and they are 'shorthand' methods of distinguishing, classifying, and resuming phases of sense-impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scientist 'refuses to project his conceptions... into the real world of perception until he has perceived them there.' Treat such conceptions as valid ideals so long as they economise thought; do not treat them as 'things-in-themselves' beyond sense-impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual existence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: By the real existence of anything we mean that it forms a more or less permanent group of sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assert perceptual existence (i.e., that something is 'real' in perception) there must be persistent sensory impressions classifiable together (contrast ether, which lacks direct grouped sense-impressions). If no such perceptual grouping exists, consider the entity a conception rather than a perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy/utility as criterion for postulating concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception remains valid so long as it continues to economise the scientist's thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concepts (e.g., atom, ether, geometrical surface) are introduced because they 'enable us to classify and resume' phenomena; the primary test is whether they expand the range of perceptual experience that can be described and predicted, not metaphysical truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological restraint: avoid metaphysical projection
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientist refuses to project his conceptions (atom, ether) into the real world of perception until he has perceived them there; he leaves 'things-in-themselves' to the metaphysician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use scientific conceptions to make claims about a supersensible reality; limit assertions to what is warranted by sense-impressions and the classificatory/predictive success of the conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability limits of geometrical and physical theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical truths apply with absolute accuracy to no group whatever of our sense-impressions; they enable classification and are valid where senses/instruments have sufficient keenness/precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that geometry (and similar idealised theories) works as an approximation or average: valid within limits set by sensory acuity and instrument precision. Be explicit about these limits when applying such conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical adequacy for model choice (continuity vs discontinuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose conceptions (e.g., atomic/discontinuous vs continuous models) that best enable description and formulation of sense-impressions — e.g., physicists 'can only conceive bodies to be discontinuous' because discontinuity explains elasticity, compressibility, relative motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for a conceptual framework should be based on its ability to analyse observed phenomena (elasticity, pressure, absorption/emission), not on metaphysical preference for continuity or continuity's intuitive appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulating concepts to fill explanatory gaps (ether example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicists introduce the ether — a continuity — as a conception to 'fill up the interstices' and to serve as a conduit for motions, thereby enabling classification of a wider range of sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to posulate entities (like ether) if they increase the range of phenomena that can be described; nonetheless, treat them as conceptions until perceptual evidence warrants asserting perceptual existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralism and domain-specific validity of models
rubrics_metrics.description: Two conceptions which cannot both correspond to realities in the perceptual world (e.g., geometrical surface and atom) may nevertheless both be valid as conceptions for different ranges of sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that multiple, apparently contradictory models can each 'economise thought' for different phenomena; do not infer that one model's usefulness invalidates another's applicability in its own domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual revision with knowledge growth
rubrics_metrics.description: As our knowledge grows and our senses/instruments become keener, we are compelled to widen our concepts or to add additional ones; original concepts are not necessarily invalid but may need modification or extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain openness to modifying or extending conceptions as new observations and insights arise. Historical development (e.g., from Euclidean geometry to expanded spatial concepts) illustrates this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space and time as modes of perception, not external realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Space and time are modes by which the perceptive faculty distinguishes objects (space for coexistence, time for sequence); we cannot assert a real existence for them beyond perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat space and time as organising frameworks of perception (external/internal modes) that 'arrange' sense-impressions; do not attribute to them ontological status beyond their role in perception-based science. This affects what can legitimately be postulated about the universe.
